title: The Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: The Mean Value Theorem says that if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there exists at least one c in (a, b) where f'(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a).
The MVT states that the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change at some point in the interval.
Geometrically, the MVT guarantees a point where the tangent line is parallel to the secant line connecting the endpoints of the graph.
The left side f'(c) of the MVT is the tangent slope (instantaneous rate); the right side [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a) is the secant slope (average rate).
The MVT requires continuity on the closed interval [a, b] and differentiability on the open interval (a, b); if either fails, the conclusion can fail.
Rolle's Theorem is the special case of the MVT where f(a) = f(b), guaranteeing a point c with f'(c) = 0.
To apply the MVT, verify the hypotheses, compute the average rate of change, set f'(x) equal to it, and keep solutions inside (a, b).
Example: for f(x) = x³ − 3x + 1 on [0, 2], the average rate is 1, and solving 3c² − 3 = 1 gives c = 2/√3 ≈ 1.155 in (0, 2).
A jump discontinuity can make the MVT fail because no tangent matches the secant slope, as with a step function.
A corner like f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1] satisfies continuity but not differentiability, and the MVT conclusion fails there.
The Extreme Value Theorem says that a function continuous on a closed interval [a, b] attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on that interval.
The EVT requires a closed, bounded interval; on an open interval like (0, 1) a continuous function such as f(x) = x may attain neither an absolute max nor min.
A critical point is an interior x where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) is undefined while f is defined.
Absolute extrema of a continuous function on a closed interval occur only at critical points or at the endpoints.
The Candidates Test (Closed Interval Method) evaluates f at all critical points and both endpoints, then takes the largest and smallest values.
Example: for f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x on [0, 3], the critical points are x = 1 and x = 2, and evaluating gives f(0)=0, f(1)=5, f(2)=4, f(3)=9.
In that example the absolute maximum f(3) = 9 and absolute minimum f(0) = 0 both occur at endpoints, illustrating why endpoints must be checked.
On free response, both MVT hypotheses must be stated as satisfied before applying the theorem, or the justification point is lost.
A consequence of the MVT: if f'(x) = 0 on an interval, then f is constant there, which is why two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant.
A consequence of the MVT: if f'(x) > 0 on an interval, then f is strictly increasing there, justifying the Increasing/Decreasing Test.
Toll-camera speed enforcement uses the MVT: average speed over a known distance exceeding the limit guarantees the limit was exceeded at some instant.
A common AP table problem gives values of f and asks you to justify that f'(c) equals a value; compute the average rate of change between two entries and cite the MVT.
